utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We continue this morning with the evidence of Mr. Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave an undertaking at the beginning of your evidence to speak the truth. That undertaking continues to apply to the evidence today. We'll now continue with the examination by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are your glasses all right? Is your headset on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about the return of citizens as part of the re-admission procedure which was involuntary. That's when people were forced to return to their country. Let me ask you something about the voluntary return of citizens today. Take the case of a citizen who had orderly documents previously, a passport or an ID card, previously would he have been in any danger at all of not seeing his return to the country approved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not under the condition that he was a national of that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about persons who were registered in any sort of different type of record at all, nationals of Yugoslavia with no document in their possession, would they have faced the danger of not seeing their return to Yugoslavia approved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no nationals of Yugoslavia would have run that risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed the decree on ID cards, the wartime decree, yesterday. The following issue cropped up, did this have anything to do with recruitment, with drafting people into the ranks of the army? Let me ask you this: Was this decree on ID cards relevant for both men and women, did it apply to both?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it applied to everybody who fell within the age group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this applied throughout Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This 14-year limit, in the law that applies in Yugoslavia does this have anything to do with a person's criminal liability or criminal record?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in criminal law, but I know that persons over 14 years of age can be made criminally responsible depending on their age, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about those under 14 years of age, under our law can these persons be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have Exhibit 6D1324 brought up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this exhibit something to do with the question of the change in the age for ID cards?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your suggestion is that the selection of this age has got something with the age of criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because in that decision it says to enable police to do its work easily so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but how on -- how would that relate to the fact that it was a temporary provision during the war and was abolished immediately after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: More crimes are expected during the war probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, you have 6D1324 in front of you, don't you. This is the letter that the National Council sent to counsel Dragan Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We looked at this yesterday, and we realized that Sadiku Sadija appeared to not have been recorded in the files in Kosovska Mitrovica. The question was raised of the files that burnt down or were destroyed. Can you please read for us the first paragraph, I mean number 1, since this has not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads Halimi Mahmut, father Bajram, probably, born on the 7th of April, 1954, in Donje Zabare, Kosovska Mitrovica municipality. Citizen's personal identification number 0704954922011, residing in Kosovska Mitrovica, Boska Mitrovica street, number 258, in possession of ID card number 92444 issued by the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP on the 22nd of February, 1994, serial number SR08674237, having checked the files of travel document and driving licences issued, it has been established that this person does not have a travel document or indeed a driving licence. No file on the issuance of this ID card has been preserved."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the last sentence because it has been misrecorded?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The file on ID issued has not been preserved."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is about Kosovska Mitrovica, and as you explained the files there were destroyed. In addition to that, does this not show that information on this person had been preserved in a different form and where could that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you can see the objection coming to the leading nature of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask if this witness knows which database or which files could contain this data. Because it's obvious from the document that it is found, the data can be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even that's a leading question. The question should be: What does this show about the way in which records on this person have been retained or records have been made or kept; but to contrast it with the other one and seek an explanation that's different is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, you heard the Presiding Judge, haven't you. What can you tell us about the specific files in which this information was found?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this you can see that despite the fact that some of the files had been destroyed numerous other files were preserved. It was based on the existing files that any person was free to take advantage of any of their entitlements through appropriate bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about ID card information, what file would that be, given the fact that some of them had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to these files, a book, a register, is kept where information is recorded on persons who had their ID issued to them. Based on this book or register, information could be tracked down and new files could be set up, based on which anyone could now be issued with a new ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Or rather, 6D1353. You have that document, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No translation. We'll not be going, or rather, we'll not be using it. Can you simply tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- rather, these minutes were taken by a joint committee of experts following an agreement between the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the government of the Federal Republic of Germany on the return and admission of Yugoslav and German nationals who were under an obligation to leave the respective territories of those countries. The committee of experts was established and was now responsible for implementing this agreement. They would sometimes meet to discuss any problems that arose in connection with the implementation of that agreement, and this was one of those meetings. Minutes were drawn up and delivered to all those working on the ground who were in any way involved with this process for their information so that they might be better able to adapt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of return are we looking at here, is this a forced repatriation or is this something people did of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are people who simply happened to be in this other country and now refused to return to our country. All those people happened to be our nationals, and many of them had no valid documents, travel documents, ID cards, or otherwise on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meeting held on the 30th and 31st of January, 1997, in Belgrade, and these minutes were dispatched to people working out in the field sometime in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it relates to a mutual problem, the return of Germans to Germany and the return of Yugoslavs to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, indeed, but there were no Germans in our territory that any questions were being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was ascertained in relation to these persons that they ought to return to the countries in which they had been residing. So were these people re-admitted? Did Yugoslavia admit them back in?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in keeping with the protocol and the procedures that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For this purpose, did you need accurate files and records?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had to make sure and only those who were ascertained to be our nationals were re-admitted into the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the other countries, did they rely on the checks that you performed at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was solely based on any checks and file inspections that we performed that many persons were re-admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Serbia and Montenegro, were -- was this agreement implemented separately in both of these republics?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true but the expert committee was at the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Yugoslavia had any agreements with any other countries that had been signed were in effect by this time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1997, right, because the developments were afoot at the time and I know that this was the case with Germany and Switzerland. I'm quite certain about that, I think also Sweden and Norway and negotiations were underway with a number of other countries, but I can't tell you for sure when these were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about any proceedings before any courts in those countries to send these people back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were bodies in those countries who dealt with this problem of illegal immigrants. There were a number of asylum seekers and they would then deal with any such applications. As for anything else that may have been a problem or if there were any grievances and complaints, I think such a party was free to address an appropriate court of law but I'm not privy to any detail of these procedures and other similar procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to Serbia and Kosovo now. Did you read any reports that were produced at border crossings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't often have the chance to read those reports because of the way the administration was organized. These reports normally reached the border-related affairs department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Kosovo, what were the crossings in Kosovo that people used to leave the country?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two border crossings for the most part, possibly a third, the Djeneral Jankovic road across the border, there was a rail crossing also called Djeneral Jankovic, but I'm not sure if that's what it was called; and there was Vrbnica and Globocica facing Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why other border crossings were not used if there were any?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as Cafa Prusit is concerned, the terrain is very inaccessible there and there is very little border traffic there anyway due to its geographic position. As far as I know, there weren't any proper conditions for there to be any traffic there due to the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you mean situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the danger of aggression and activities of our Defence forces, the police, army, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether there were any orders to have documents taken away; however, from the administration where you worked were the border police stations ever ordered to seize motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no order was ever such received. I'm sorry, motor vehicles are not within the jurisdiction of this administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there situations when people from other lines of work of the Ministry of the Interior were at border crossings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would happen that sometimes people would come from the administration of the crime police or from the territorial organ, people who were in charge of this subject matter from time to time, members of the State Security Service would come as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a border crossing where the entire police station was there awaiting the entry of NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was at Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during their trip, or rather, in agreement with NATO they prepared for transport, for their trip, and together with the units they moved along the road to Pristina. In a way, they provided security for them, and then on one part of the road, I don't know exactly which one, they were stopped by some other unit and the commander of this unit said that this was not the same unit with which they had travelled from the border. That is where they were disarmed and all their police equipment was taken away, all their weapons, and also some TV crews recorded this, filmed it, and it could even be viewed on different satellite channels that could be viewed in Belgrade. We had the opportunity of seeing this moment in particular. At that moment that was the only information we had about what the fate was of our people at this border crossing because we did not have any other communication with them. Only when the commander arrived in Belgrade did he give us some more detailed information about all this that I have been telling you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't understand what this is about. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the time when the forces entered after the signing of the Kumanovo agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that's been recorded is: Was there a single border crossing where the entire police station was there, even when the NATO aggression took place? That's rather different than the situation after the Kumanovo agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I never used the word "aggression," but anyways --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is to do with escorting NATO troops into the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. They just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to go over this again then because I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What period is this about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the period after the Kumanovo Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What forces entered and from where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case from the direction of Macedonia, the road that crosses the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. Forces entered, I don't know exactly from which state, from which NATO member country they were, I think they were American troops, and even the officer, the commander of these units previously established contact with our commander and he asked about a liaison officer from our side who was supposed to meet us -- meet them there. He mentioned a name that our commander did not know, and then this officer waited there for a while and then when time became critical he agreed with this officer that they would have to enter anyway, they prepared their equipment and weapons and practically they did that, they handed over the border crossing to them, and then they started moving into the interior in a convoy, they made a convoy out of their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So part of NATO forces were moving with them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were moving down the road and they were allowed to move only when they told them that it was safe to move and that's how they moved to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, did they hand over the border police station to these forces when these forces entered the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire station and all its equipment, technical equipment, of course, and this kind of a station cannot function without such technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that they took their weapons and what else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons, possibly some of the records they could carry that are very important. This is a reference to our internal records and their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If an offence or crime is revealed at a border crossing, who takes over the case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the complexity of the case involved. If the policemen at the border crossing cannot deal with this on their own, then they inform the line of work from the territorial SUP, and then they take over the case and the persons who are believed to be the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina, was there always a member of the administration for foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a member of the line of work of the administration, but in some situations it was an officer or a police official who worked at the headquarters of the admission but it could have been a police official who had been sent from another secretariat too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and up until the end, do you know who these persons were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, for example, Dobrica Vesic was there, he's a police official from the administration from the border police; then after that, I cannot give you the exact dates, though, it was Mr. Vucurevic, Radovan Vucurevic, he was the head of department of the border police in the Novi Sad SUP; after that I think it was Petar Bogdanovic from the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a special methodology of work with the staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had very few contacts with the staff. For the most part we directly communicated with our own people within our own line of work, that's far more efficient. I could only call Vucurevic or some other official to help me, but that would considerably slow down the proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So where did work orders come to the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come only from the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are they responsible to, these stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did the border police stations cooperate with in their own territory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cooperated with all the organs that were present there in that territory along all the lines of work in the secretariat of the interior and everybody else with whom it was necessary to cooperate on any matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: An employee within your line of work who was on the staff, say Mr. Vucurevic, was he within the chain of orders, "nalog," or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not issue any order, "nalog," to any line of work without the knowledge of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to the commander of the Vrbnica border police station after the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the withdrawal from Kosovo all of them reported to the administration and I had occasion to talk to Mr. Ognjenovic, I think that's his name, Ognjenovic, yes, I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anything characteristic in terms of what it was that he told you then about what had happened at the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I found characteristic was that we got information then that -- from the horse's mouth that the situation was very unpleasant, that there were a lot of people, a lot of vehicles, that it was impossible to carry out any checks over these persons. And what was very characteristic in my memory was that these persons threw away their personal documents, if they did have them on them. However, these persons had not been searched. It is possible that they had kept some documents; however, these details could not have been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Pristina on official business in 1999 and 2000?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 I was in Pristina on official business after the withdrawal, after the Kumanovo Agreement. We had a service there that carried out the work of the civilian administration for the needs of the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, issuing personal documents to citizens who wanted to resolve this matter there on the spot in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time who was the head of your administration when you went down there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly now. I went to Pristina twice after that. I really cannot say what the date was. I don't know if Mr. Lukic was already head of administration then or whether I was still in charge of the administration, I don't know exactly when this happened. But I just know that Mr. Misic, assistant minister, phoned me and said to me that I should go there and report at this coordinating body, I think that's what it was called -- Andjelkovic, Andjelkovic headed this body, he's a politician, Andjelkovic. And the task was to view the possibilities of having citizens issued with travel documents in Pristina, and that this should be done in agreement with UNMIK. So then I went with this Mr. Andjelkovic and I attended a meeting with the representatives of UNMIK where these details were agreed upon and where practically we did receive approval to the effect that we could issue such documents. And then I simply looked at the technical possibilities and some internal details as to how this could be carried through, and that is what was agreed upon, that that is the way we would act. Before that some documents had already been issued in terms of registering vehicles, driver's licences, and so on and so forth, and from that moment onwards travel documents were issued as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Until when did that work in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly up until which moment this worked. I know that something changed. I think that by then I wasn't working at the administration, but things changed when our employee who was responsible for that there got killed, Mr. Aleksandar Petrovic, he was killed in a terrorist action in Pristina. And after that there were some problems, but I'm not aware of any details because by then I wasn't working at the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were documents issued at the same time to Albanians at the relocated secretariats of the interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons who asked for documents to be issued to them, either at these points in Pristina or elsewhere -- I mean, there were two other points in Kosovo Polje and at Gracanica and also at the relocated locations. I do not have information about the persons who were seeking these documents, but everyone was entitled to exercise their own rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the relocation, after Petrovic was killed, was this taken out of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, you're not. On the basis of what were these documents being issued now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were being issued on the basis of details contained in the records that could have been provided by the employees who were working at the relocated locations. Requests were only received in Pristina, and then they were processed at the relocated locations in Nis and then the completed travel documents were returned and handed over to the persons who had filed the requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic background was of these persons who had personal documents issued to them, say, in Kosovo and Metohija after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Pristina location?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pristina and you said there were two more.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, for the most part I know quite reliably so that most of them were ethnic Albanians, but I think that there were other persons too. There were Serbs who lived down there as well and members of other ethnic groups. So however, due to the actual numbers, since the Albanian population was prevalent, most of these persons were Albanians too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did UNMIK issue its own passports at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when UNMIK actually started issuing travel documents. I didn't have an opportunity to actually learn something about those documents. It may have been after I left the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the multi-ethnic police force established after the end of the air-strikes in the south of Serbia and could you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know quite a lot about that because I was personally involved in the project to develop this whole concept of the creation of the multi-ethnic police force for Bujanovac, Presevo, and Medvedja municipalities. And afterwards in the late stages of the development of this project I ran the training of the multi-ethnic police force as a co-manager together with the OSCE representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was at the head of the public security sector at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he approach this as something that was purely formal or did he really devote all his efforts to it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that he took this in a perfunctory manner because he talked to me before he sent me down there and he underscored the importance of this project. I saw him visit Bujanovac several times. He visited the people working down there, the MUP representatives, and on during the training upon his decision, the whole training was carried out, the whole programme was approved by him, and during the training I think that he attended all the graduation ceremonies because there were four generations of people who graduated and he attended each and every ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where did this training take place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the training for the people who were already in the police, they underwent an abridged course, that was in the police stations in Bujanovac, Presevo, and Medvedja, and for the new recruits it was in Mitrovo Polje near Krusevac, somewhere between Krusevac and Kraljevo. That was the location that was selected for the training of new recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how did the OSCE evaluate this project?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know the project received very positive marks because this was the first time that Serbs and Albanians were able to work together on the same job thanks to this project, and I think that the situation in fact is -- this is still the case. So this project was very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P1505 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we don't have it in our bundle. I will not be asking you about the contents of this document. I will just ask you something about the paragraph above the word "decision." We're trying to establish here whether the MUP staff was an auxiliary body or an organizational unit of the MUP. Did we go through those legal provisions in the course of the proofing and what did we establish what powers did the -- whoever issued this decision exercise, what legislation is this based on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we went through it and we realized that the legal provisions contained in the Ministry on the Internal Affairs empowers the minister, that in the course of management of certain organs that he can issue orders, instructions, and establish some bodies in order to facilitate the performance of this function. But it does not form the basis for the establishment of an internal organizational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had he wanted to establish an organizational unit, would he have had to use some other legal provisions, some other article from this law?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some other article, but I would have to now go through the law to look for this article, perhaps Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe this part of the law?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which one. Could you please refer me to the actual article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not now bother you with this. We will call a judge to testify, so if necessary we will go back to this issue with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please have in e-court Exhibit 6D130.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps I missed it, but could counsel indicate whether or not this -- we were notified of this in accordance with the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Notified about 6D130? It should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you now have this document in front of you. Who is sending this dispatch, can we see this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian MUP, the public security department. It is signed by assistant to the minister, Stojan Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who is this sent to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is sent to the federal MUP for their information, because this pertains to the implementation of the federal law. I guess it's the Law on Foreigners, foreign nationals, and all these SUPs in the field, from 1 to 33; and all the border police stations in the field, to their commanders; to the MUP staff in Pristina, to the head; and to all organizational units at the headquarters, the police administration, the traffic police administration, the crime police administration, the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the orders, "nalog," who are they issued to, who was the recipient of them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just browsed through and I can see that all those orders pertain to some action that has to be taken by the SUPs, the organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior, and possibly of the border police stations if they came to be in a situation where they would have to actually implement some of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This pertains to the updating of the lists of foreigners with permanent residence and foreigners with temporary residence permits and all the other preparations so that they may be forcibly escorted to the state border and deported from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or escorted to a reception centre set up for this purpose. So we're starting with the updating of the lists. Is it possible for the staff to do anything pursuant to this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no. The staff can't do anything. They don't have those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who has those lists, the lists that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we're talking about foreigners who have residence in our country, and every territorial organ or the internal organizational unit that deals with the foreign nationals has to keep its records updated, the records of the foreigners who have been allowed to stay in the country for a longer period of time. I'm not talking about tourists. They merely have to report and register that they are there, but now we're talking about foreigners who were given residence permits valid for a longer period of time for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any reception centres for foreign nationals in our country before this period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before this period there were such reception centres. There is one in Padinska Skila, it's operational now too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether other states have such reception centres for foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically anything about that, but it is quite logical that every state should have such a reception centre because it is quite conceivable that a foreigner who is there illegally cannot leave the territory of that country until everything has been done to enable him to do so, and then he has to stay somewhere. These are usually semi-open facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will move on to another document, but could you please just memorise the number of this dispatch, it's 1352, is it not? The date is the 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 6D1373.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see this document in front of you. The number is 1373.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is sending this list?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is just a list, an updated list of foreign nationals who have the permanent residence and who are temporarily resident in the territory of the secretariat. So this organ complied with our dispatch, the number is 1352. You can see the reference here in this document. So this list was made and it is kept on their files. They don't have any obligation to send it to anyone. I don't know whether they sent it to us or not, but if they did, it was just for our information. But I believe that they didn't send it. And you can see here for every person the status, whether they have permanent residence or temporary residence, whether they are married to a Yugoslav national or whatever the basis is for their residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, I don't have any further questions for you. Thank you for coming here and testifying. I think that some of my colleagues may have some questions for you, and after that you will be cross-examined by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I have a short cross-examination of this witness, but before I start, as we have been hearing evidence and the issue of ID card has been brought up. I thought maybe it would have been for the benefit of the Judges to actually see the specimen of the ID. Well, due to the fact that in this time constraint or short time that I had, I had to use mine. So it is uploaded in the e-court and it will be, if you -- I would offer that under seal until we have time to redact it and then -- because I'm interested only in the specimen of it. And then it will be filed as a public document. I have talked to my learned friend Mr. Hannis -- Mr. Stamp over there, and he doesn't object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds as though that would be helpful, Mr. Zecevic, and there are clearly understandable reasons for it being under seal until another example can be found and uploaded. So we will allow you to proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I must say another thing. I'm sorry, of course we couldn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't provide the translation, but I believe we can do it as the witness can read through it and it is very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have 1D775 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dujkovic. Mr. Dujkovic, this is the ID card, it is in fact my ID card, and now I would like us to go through this ID card slowly to explain the form itself and I would like to ask you to read very slowly so that everything can be interpreted into English. Mr. Dujkovic, please tell me what we see here in e-court, what is this? Do you see the image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I -- I have it printed out, so maybe we could be helped with the -- could you please give this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please explain to us very briefly each of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first photograph, that's the cover of the document. You can see the coat of arms, that's the coat of arms of the SFRY, and you can see the words "personal ID card" in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go on to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just very slowly. Just look at the monitor in front of you. So what does it say here in the upper left-hand corner, we can see the coat of arms and what does it say beneath it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is again the coat of arms of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and you can see the name of the state, and it says underneath the Socialist Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, could you please tell me, this is obviously the form for a document that was valid in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every republic of the former SFRY printed out this form in the language that was in current usage in that particular republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This personal ID card was issued in 1999, as we're about to see.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain why they were still using forms from the SFRY at the time, and when was that changed, the header and the coat of arms, if you remember? When was it changed to reflect the new name, the FRY?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was still in use because the law probably still applied on the unified information database concerning IDs that had been adopted by the then-SFRY. I can't really give you the exact date when this was changed, when the regulation was amended, to reflect the new name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us go now to the first line of this document. We see a parenthesis there and what does it say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next one?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Name."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Last name, name of parent, date of birth," and then under two separate lines, "place of birth, municipality, province, republic." The last thing is "blood type."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The other page that we see on the screen there's a photograph there, as we can see, there's a stamp on it; and next to the photograph there's some sort of a number, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the citizen's personal identification number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain about that number, please, briefly. What does it comprise and what is it used for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each citizen is assigned a number like that at birth. This is something that is determined in the birth register and rubber stamped by the appropriate branch of the Ministry of the Interior, wherever the person happens to reside. The first digit are used to indicate the date of birth, the 30th of March, 1959, so there's the sequence there, the day, the month, and the year. The remaining digits are a matter of internal classification, I suppose this is something about the Republic of Serbia, the number is 71, and then the remaining digits are all used for different purposes and to signify a number of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If my understanding is correct, the first seven digits reflect the date, month, and year of birth of the person under this number?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just underneath those two lines, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Place of residence and address, validity or expiry date. On the left the register number, the number from the book that we mentioned during my evidence, where every application is recorded in chronological order. On the right, the date the ID card was issued. The signature of an authorised official and an official stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, these numbers printed in red, what do they mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the serial number of the document, the printers give each document a special number, the people at the print works, each new document gets a new number like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I move on, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have -- [Interpretation] Can we please turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please comment, read what it says, what the page reflects, and comment on what it means, what it's in reference to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we see a number of other categories. Information is recorded here regarding the address of the holder, any changes in address or residence. For example, a person residing in Belgrade, they want to move to a different city now and this change of address would have been recorded in that next line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We see something marked in pen there. Can you just read what it says.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Place and municipality of residence," that's what the reference is to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the first line?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the second line is "street and street number" in this new place of residence. On the left is the date this change was entered, and on the right we see a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the signature of an authorised official, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the remaining five categories, they are identical to those preceding them, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, for example, we see this address stated here, and someone decides to move to a new address, this new address is recorded on the next line, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Next page, please, page 4 in this case, photograph number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On the left we see the same thing continued, change of address, flat, street number, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those are the three boxes that we can see, categories that we can see on the left, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to read the remarks on the right-hand page slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Remark: It is the right and duty of every citizen over 18 years of age to have an ID card. "Each person is entitled to no more than one ID card. "The holder of an ID card is under an obligation to keep the ID card on their person at all times and to produce it when necessary and when required to do so by the -- an authorised official. "It is prohibited to lend an ID card to any other person, to use another person's ID card as one's own, or to misuse this document in any other way. "A person whose physical appearance changes to a significant degree over time so that the person's appearance is no longer identical to the one displayed on their ID photo or a person who has his or her name changed is under an obligation within 15 days of the time such change occurs to apply for a new ID. "Any person misplacing or losing their ID card must immediately and at the latest within 15 days report this to the municipal body of the Ministry of the Interior and apply for a new ID card."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dujkovic, these remarks or observations, they're actually legal provisions, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is something that is actually stated in the law and these are remarks telling persons what to do with their ID cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move to something else but -- and I'm willing if Your Honours would like me to give an additional or maybe ask the witness to give an additional explanation if you need one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know one is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, if I remember correctly you said yesterday that you started working for the MUP or the SUP in 1980, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've been with the police since 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, right, 1971, my apologies. So you were with the police back in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence, were there any decree laws that were passed when a state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that and this had to do with wartime plans that were produced or kept at various levels. As for my own police station of which I later became commander of another such police station, so I was personally in charge of keeping or producing these plans, and that's why I know about this. One of the things that these plans included were decree laws, but those were draft laws, before being adopted, and they were there for the eventuality that they might have to be signed and put into practice and they were there for us as guidance so that we would know what to do just in case. Those decrees were, for the most part, there to replace any laws that concerned the work of the Ministry of the Interior. More specifically, those that concerned the work of any organizational unit keeping or producing a plan like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what at least some of those were in reference to or should I ask you a more specific question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this because those were the regulations that I myself and my police station were in charge of implementing. This was about border checks along the border facing Hungary, Subotica specifically. Those were decree laws, the first of those being in reference to the crossing of state borders and monitoring any movement within the border belt. There was another that was in reference to the movement and residence of the foreign nationals. The third was in reference to travel documents belonging to Yugoslavia's nationals, and there may have been other decrees related to the laws that fell under our purview, but these three were the most important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there another decree that was envisaged, a decree on ID cards and change of address during a state of war in the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there was such a decree, but I'm just not certain that this decree was something that fell under my purview; but I know that a regulation like that existed, I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you happen to know, since you are a lawyer by profession, which body it was that passed these decree laws?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether it was the government or perhaps another body such as the president or such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm about to show you to dispel any doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P1623 brought up in e-court. This is the Constitution of the SFRY and the relevant Article is 317. Article 317, I apologise, I'm not sure about the page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the witness has said that he doesn't know the answer to the question. It is a matter of law. Is it really necessary to put a document to him when it's part of the process on which you can make submissions anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is not essential. I just wanted to in all fairness to the witness because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, what would be helpful to us would be if he did have experience and could tell us what had actually happened. But just to ask him to read the law and say what it means is not really a very useful exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, do you know that the Kingdom of Holland has a regulation saying that all persons over 14 years of age must have an ID card?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about that type of regulation in any other European country?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no knowledge of that specifically, but I know that the age limit varies from country to country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try and be briefer than Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dujkovic. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I represent General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You testified in chief with Mr. Lukic and you talked about the fact that you were part of the re-admission procedure based on an agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Germany, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We look at an exhibit dated 1997. What I want to know is whether this re-admission procedure was in progress in 1998 and 1999 as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was formally still in progress and it went on for as long as air traffic could go on. I can't specify the time, but it was probably until just before the air-strikes against our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about up until that point in time, had you been in touch with your German colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the committee of experts, which was a permanent body. This was something for the federal Ministry of the Interior to deal with. We from the republican ministry seconded some of our members to aid the work of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, I would like you to look at 5D1, it's a Defence exhibit. We are now waiting for it to be brought up in e-court, and as we're waiting let me tell you that these are extracts from official German documents obtained, or rather, something that was obtained by the International Association of Lawyers Against Nuclear Armament. This was published in German daily Junge Welt on the 24th of April, 1994. There are extracts here from seven decisions taken by federal courts in Germany. I think you mentioned in chief that it was the administrative courts that ruled such matters as those related to applications made by asylum seekers. What I'd like you to do now is this. Let us have a look at the opinion rendered by the Muenster Higher Administrative Court on the 11th of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is no foundation in the evidence so far that entitles this witness to be commenting about judgements in a German federal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to be the same point, Mr. Bakrac, as with Mr. Zecevic. It's a matter of law and interpretation for us. This document has, in fact, been admitted and you can address us about it. But the witness has already told you that he doesn't have any personal knowledge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that the situation is similar to the one that Mr. Zecevic had. I just wanted to ask the witness whether from his personal contacts with German colleagues, because we did hear about that before I showed this document, that he had personal contacts with them, whether these -- this information that he received through his personal contacts correspond to one of these positions. That was one of my questions. Secondly, at the very beginning of this trial when this was admitted into evidence, you suggested that we try to find some judgements and the Defence did find four judgements. Roman numerals IV, V, VI, and VII, they have PD [as interpreted] numbers and right now they are being translated from German into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has said that the contacts were maintained through the committee of experts. There is no indication, this is Mr. Stamp's point, there is no indication of any foundation for the witness referring to these German judgements. You would need to have shown that he had some personal knowledge to which these could be relevant. Now what is it you're saying he knows about this? There's no indication that he has any practical experience of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to clarify that now and see whether the witness knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, when you talked to your German colleagues on this expert committee, did you get any information about the reasons why administrative courts refused requests for asylum placed by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is based on the work of these expert committees and also the previous period when the agreements were being negotiated. The basic problem then was whether it was safe for such persons to return to our country, and also there were some technical financial problems as to whether this could be carried through. The safety problem was dealt with even in the initial stage, in particular during the implementation; otherwise, these persons could not have been returned if either one of the two parties believed that their safety would be jeopardized. I know that proceedings were initiated for each and every individual to have asylum granted or not. I do not know how many cases were approved, but I know that over 90 per cent were not because at that time the figure that was bandied about was 150.000 persons who were supposed to be sent back. And these administrative proceedings probably had to do with an appeal or something like that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is sufficient for me by way of an explanation. I don't know if we need to elaborate on this any further with this witness, and I kindly ask you for instructions with regard to the four judgements that we have received. Can I refer to them now and will they just be marked for identification until we receive a translation or should we tender them into evidence through a separate motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They seem to deal with something different from what the witness is dealing with. The witness is dealing with the situation on the ground, whether it's safe for persons to be returned from Germany to Yugoslavia because they've been refused admission. The judgements themselves, however, deal with the reason for denying -- I assume they deal with the reason for denying asylum, and the witness knows nothing about that from the answer he's just given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely in these judgements refusing asylum we see that conditions have not been met because there is the requirement that has been met, namely, that it is safe for these persons to return and they will not be persecuted in the original state, and I wanted to ask this witness about his contacts with his German colleagues, namely, that asylum had been rejected because it was not unsafe to return to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. The last thing the witness said before it scrolls off is in respect to these which he I think he supposes that they're administrative proceedings to do with appeal or something like that, I really don't know. That's the last thing he said about these administrative hearings or judgements, he doesn't know what they're about. So this is not the witness to be inquiring into decisions in a foreign court or these particular decisions. He doesn't know anything about their sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- you've had adequate opportunity, Mr. Bakrac, to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We agree that you should be permitted to ask the question you wish to ask, in view of the basis for these decisions. The issue of weight is quite a separate matter and the issue of the exact interpretation of the judgements may be a separate matter also. But if the witness is permitted to read something from these and explain whether it's consistent with his personal knowledge of the circumstances, then that seems to us to be a relevant exercise of cross-examination. So please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How much longer will your cross-examination be?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am just going to select one judgement very briefly, one sentence. If you allow me, I will read it out, and that would be my last question, namely, whether this corresponds to the experience he had while working on this commission. It is the judgement under Roman numeral VII, PD1238 [as interpreted] is its number, but this is a separate matter. The 11th of March, 1999, the opinion of the higher court in Muenster, ethnic Albanians in Kosovo have neither been nor are now exposed to local or country-wide group persecution in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does this position of the administrative court in Muenster correspond to your own experience in direct contacts and talks with your German colleagues and experience on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only condition on which such an agreement could have been reached and implemented, that their return would be safe and that they were not persecuted, but that they were in second or third countries for some other reasons and that is when they sought asylum. In our jargon we called them false asylum seekers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that the re-admission process lasted all the way up until the 24th of March, 1999, when the bombing started and while there were still flights. So did the Germans return these people and were they returned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every day on all flights, on all Yugoslav airlines primarily, thousands of them were returned and big groups were returned to Belgrade airport, Pristina airport, and they were taken to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions and before the break, if you allow me, could I please ask you to instruct me as to what I'm supposed to do about these four judgements. I can have them marked for identification until the translation and completed, and I believe that will be within about ten days. That is what I was told. I can give you four numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I have misunderstood. I thought the whole document had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, PD1 [as interpreted] -- and there are four judgements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- 5D11 -- that's the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a free-standing document containing the excerpts from seven judgements. When this document was originally introduced, your suggestion was that if we could find these judgements in their entirety, that that would be useful for the Trial Chamber. Finally we did manage somehow to find four judgements out of the seven existing ones, and those are the ones that pertain to IV, V, VI, and VII respectively those paragraphs of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Their number is 5D1368 did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, 5D1235, 5D1236, 5D1237, and 5D1238. I just used one of them when putting a question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will give you a decision on that when we return after the break. Mr. Dujkovic, we need a break at this stage, that will be for 20 minutes. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher, please, while we have the break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, we will mark for identification the one of these judgements that was referred to and put to the witness, that's 5D1235. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, 5D1238 was the one that was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall mark that one for identification and we shall refuse to admit the others as unnecessary. So you will have to have that one translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just want to inform Your Honours that corrected statement of this witness is now entered into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall allow it to be substituted for the existing English version -- sorry, the existing version of both. In fact, there was a page missing from one of them, I think the English version as well. So your updated one will cure both points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dujkovic. Firstly I would like to just quickly have a look at some of the documents that are referred to in your statement and clear up one or two things. In paragraph 13 of your statement you refer to 6D459. Could we have it in e-court, please. And you have a copy there I assume. You said that it is seen here that Urosevac SUP directly informed the MUP without informing the staff. Can you just indicate to me in which part of the document it is indicated that it was being sent to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please repeat the number, 6D459, I have the criminal report filed against a customs service official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I think it's 549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness's own statement is 6D1499.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm referring to the document that he mentions in paragraph 13 thereof, 6D459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, it seems to be in that document that it is sent from the Urosevac SUP to the public prosecutor, but you seem to make a point that it is sent directly to the MUP without going to the staff. I just wanted you to tell us where on the document, I seem to have missed that, it is indicated that it is sent to the MUP from the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness should be shown page number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we need 6D459 on the screen, please, page number 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the documents under this number is a dispatch sent by the Urosevac SUP, the crime police department, to the Serbian MUP to the administration of the crime police, that's the way I read it and that's what we can see here on the screen. The number is not indicated here. The communications service fixes the number when the dispatch is actually sent, but of course the case itself has its own KU number, reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What page of your document is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about this part of the document that we can see on the screen, and I have it here, it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page has the identification of the persons or offices to whom the document is sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the point, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted to find out where it is that it was sent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the page we were on looked as though it was being sent to the administration in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that there's a problem with the translation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but the page in English is not the same. This is part of the criminal report. Perhaps it's some other page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I could move on. I think the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, let's get this dealt with. What is the problem here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness is showing us something that exists in the Serbian version which is not in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's get the same page in English until we see what ... Well, these two pages are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're right, Mr. Stamp. We will have to move on. Apparently there are three different entries in e-court, and that's what's causing the difficulty. Mr. Lukic, there seems to be an abundance of material under this number that goes beyond the subject matter of the one on the left of the screen, but we'll try to find the right one and then Mr. Stamp can return to it later. So continue with something else, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 you referred to a document in which -- which relates to a post office worker being arrested for ex -- well, for taking money unlawfully from Albanians in respect to exit taxes. Was it a normal practice for Albanians to charge -- to be charged exit taxes to leave Albania during the armed NATO intervention? For Kosovar Albanians to be charged exit taxes to leave Kosovo during the NATO intervention, was that a regular practice?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not levied only on Albanians; it was levied on all persons and it had nothing to do with the aggression. I don't have the document here in front of me, but I suppose that those were exit taxes that were introduced by the state and these were introduced a number of years before this period. Every person that was supposed -- that wanted to travel abroad had to pay a certain tax or a fee to the state, and this had nothing to do with the actual territory, the ethnic background of the traveller, or the actual state of affairs in the state at that time, state of war or whatever. And here it is indicated, it shows from -- this actually shows that the state authorities protected each and every citizen regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just focus on the question I'm asking you. The Albanians, the Kosovar Albanians who left, the document is 6D460, I should indicate, the Kosovar Albanians who left left Kosovo during the NATO intervention in 1999, was it the norm that they were charged exit taxes at the border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Kosovo Albanians who left in the extraordinary circumstances and without any particular control, they were not subject to any controls and they did not have to pay any taxes or fees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could move to paragraph 20 of your statement, and it refers to Exhibit 6D475.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that be brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the 13th of June, 1999. You say it was signed by Obrad Stevanovic on behalf of the staff. Did you actually see a signed copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the second page of the -- of both of them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The copy we have in B/C/S here doesn't seem to be signed. Did you actually see in preparation for this statement a signed copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I saw this version that is on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
