utterances.text: Okay. So it's a mistake here when you say that the dispatch was signed by Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was probably printed out on the computer, it was probably saved on the computer, and the signed version was sent to the communications service so that it could then be sent on to other addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, it seems to be speculative. And the last thing I want to ask you about is at paragraph 22 of your statement where you refer to Exhibit 6D464, do you have that document in front of you? The point you make here is that the staff was not informed about this criminal report. Is this the record of what is, in fact, a misdemeanour, disciplinary report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here: "Approval to file a misdemeanour report."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And therefore, your point would be having regard to this document is that the staff was not informed in relation to filing misdemeanour reports against police officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both misdemeanour and criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where a criminal report for a serious charge, like murder, arson on someone's dwelling, is filed against a police officer in Kosovo for example, wouldn't that be something that would be managed by the SUP for the municipality in which the crime is revealed or investigated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the SUP has authority over that or jurisdiction, but they have to report any such events to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of meetings convened before and during the NATO intervention by General Lukic on behalf of the staff for Kosovo and Metohija in which leaders of the SUP, chiefs of the SUPs, made reports about investigations of crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I inspected some documents during the proofing, documents that pertained to meetings of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Listen to me again. I'm not talking about documents now. Maybe you should close your folder. I'm just asking you now: Are you aware that meetings were convened by General Lukic on behalf of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija where SUP chiefs from Kosovo and Metohija attended and gave reports about crime in their municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was not aware of what the staff was actually doing and how the reporting went and how those meetings or briefings were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the time were you aware of the official documents, official decisions, setting up the ministry staff for Kosovo and Metohija and appointing the members of it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just know that the staff was established and I know some of the members, in particular those in whose appointment I was involved; but as for the decision, the specific decision, this is not something that I had the opportunity to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you see these decisions where your subordinate Mr. Vucurevic was appointed to the staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I do know that he received a decision regarding his appointment, and I know that because I myself wrote the recommendation. And he could not have been sent there without this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to send Mr. Vucurevic, Mr. Dujkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucurevic was a member of the staff and he was to monitor the situation in the field regarding the -- any problems that pertained to the work of the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would that not be dealt with in the ordinary way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the complex security situation in the field, there was this need for a person to be there to assist and facilitate the execution of the tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Someone from your administration, though, would be based in the SUP Pristina office, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, at the Pristina SUP there were the police officers who were in the Pristina SUP and they did tasks that pertained to the border and foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic was previously based in Nis -- sorry, Novi Sad --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Novi Sad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- yes, Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vucurevic was chief of the section in the Novi Sad SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, was there not a similar section in the Pristina SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the very same section existed in the Pristina SUP, but Mr. Vucurevic was tasked with dealing with this issue in the area broader than that covered by the Pristina SUP, in the area of the whole of the province.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So his role, he was tasked with facilitating, to quote you, the execution of tasks in the whole of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the purview of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he was tasked with facilitating the MUP staff that he was appointed to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had his specific tasks related to the purview of the border police administration, and he primarily had to deal with those issues, issues that anyone from the administration going to that area would be dealing with. But I don't know what other tasks he had in the staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if we could look at P1505.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you were shown this document earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it suitable to go back to 459 or do you want to do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we have that now, Mr. Haider? I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp, it hasn't been resolved. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at 1505, this is an order of the Minister Stojiljkovic, and you will see there it includes Major Radovan Vucurevic as a member of the staff. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't you have a copy of that document with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the second page you see that Major Vucurevic is appointed by the ministry to be a member of that staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the name of Radovan Vucurevic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you go down to item 2 you will see that the minister orders or decides: "The staff is tasked with planning, organizing, and managing the activities and use of the organizational units of the ministry." So you will agree with me that Major Vucurevic, his role on the staff was to facilitate the staff as far as the border units and his area of operations were concerned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his role to facilitate the work of the administration along this line of work in this area. And he did not have a management function. He could not manage the work of the organizational units dealing with those issues, and he could not have managed or ran the work of the police stations, the border police stations, in this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he ran the work of the border police stations on a daily basis. Let me ask you this: You knew the Minister Stojiljkovic, was he a person who in your experience made formal, written decisions with specific orders that were not intended to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you probably meant Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic, and I heard the name Stojkovic in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Minister Stojiljkovic. Based on your experience as a senior official of the ministry, was he the sort of minister who made orders in that type of idle way or does specifically designating roles without an intention that they be carried out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot say what his intentions were or what decisions the minister issued, but every decision, as a rule, had to be carried out if it was lawful. A decision tantamount to an order to commit a crime must not be complied with or executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic said that you telephoned him and told him that he was being transferred to Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic was sent temporarily to Kosovo pursuant to a decision of the public security sector head, and this was done pursuant to a written recommendation by the administration chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, I asked you if you telephoned him and told him that he had been assigned to Kosovo. That's what he came and said. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what he said, then it must be accurate because usually first you have a telephone or oral conversation that precedes the formal appointment. I probably must have phoned him to see whether he was available to go there, whether he had any personal or family reasons not to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So having regard to this order of the minister that you said would be carried out unless it was illegal, what was Major Vucurevic being sent to do as a member of the staff? What were you sending him to Kosovo to do as a member of this staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was always a representative of the administration in the staff at all times, so this was not only the case for this composition of the staff when Vucurevic was there. But if I may be allowed to note one thing as far as the names that are listed here, I'm not sure whether that was really true, or rather, some of the names are unfamiliar to me. That may be some kind of an extended composition. But regardless of all that, Vucurevic's task was to facilitate the work of the administration with his work, to coordinate the work of the organizational units in Kosovo. And he may have been issued a specific task or a special task from the administration. But as far as I can recall, he was specifically tasked with liaising with the international humanitarian and other organizations that were present in that area in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive reports from Vucurevic as to his work on the staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having contacted him by telephone and sent him to Kosovo, did you speak with him during his tenure in Kosovo about his work on the staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have spoken with him, but I can't say when or for what reason. Mostly whenever he needed to see someone from the administration he would call up some line of work. This was more on a professional basis to deal with a specific problem. Orders, orders as in, "nalog," and instructions would go directly to the administration and its organizational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, was he sent to Kosovo as some sort of punishment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I move on can we look at -- quickly at 6D770 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, who was -- who did he replace, Mr. Dujkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He replaced Dobrica Vesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly at 6D770.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's another document you referred to in your statement which I had intended to ask about. It's a document from the head of the staff - I see you have it there in front of you - Major General Lukic to the chiefs of the secretariat of the interior in Kosovo and Metohija. And you see him in this document issuing tasks. Do you know under what authority as chief of the Pristina -- of the staff for Kosovo and Metohija he could issue tasks and instructions to the MUP chiefs of secretariats?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, should we ask the witness to leave before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, there is an objection being taken which we have to determine; while we do that, could you leave the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness said that he didn't know how the MUP staff functioned at that time, and if he's asked about it everything should be presented to him. The source for this is visible at paragraph 1 of this dispatch where it says: "In accordance with dispatch of chief of the public security sector," so if it's ordered by the chief of the public security sector it's obvious that he has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, what you're saying actually amounts to evidence and he's an experienced official who should be able to read this document and give the answer you've -- explanation you've given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have to give him time to read the document, not ask him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you could also deal with it in re-examination. It's for Mr. Stamp to decide how to deal with it. But an experienced official like him should be able to read the entry into this that leads up the various tasks fairly simply. But Mr. Stamp will bear in mind what you've said and deal with the -- his questions. But there is no reason why the witness should not be capable of dealing with the issue that you identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's have him back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've dealt with that matter, Mr. Dujkovic. We can now proceed. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. There's a document that is referred to in your statement, and I take it that you had an opportunity to review the document when you were giving your statement, and in that document you see General Lukic issuing tasks to the chiefs of the SUPs for Kosovo. Do you know under what authority he could issue a task to the chiefs of the SUPs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local bodies are reminded of their legal commitment in this document. The regulations that they have a commitment to are listed in this document, and that should be -- should have been clear even without this document. What I'm trying to say is what I said a while ago, representatives of the appropriate lines of work should facilitate the performance of the MUP in the area given the complex nature of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know under what authority he issues these instructions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could only have been a decision in terms of authority, a decision by the minister or whoever dispatched him, chief of the public security sector or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the very last part of your answer, please, the interpret missed. After you referred to the chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned him in a context, because I'm not certain at the time who passed the decision to dispatch Mr. Lukic on these missions, whether it was the minister or the chief of the sector; about the Chiefs of Staff, I know that it was the chief of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And couldn't that decision not be the same one you were shown, P1505, signed by Minister Stojiljkovic, which clearly empowers him to manage the affairs of the various police units in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in practice it wasn't the case that someone took over those organizational units from the staff. In my line of work we were directly in touch with all the organizational units in local SUPs in terms of business to do with the border and foreign nationals and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said you knew Mr. Ognjenovic in your line of work in the border police. Do you recall speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the commander of the police station, and this police station was part of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said you spoke with him after the war. Do you remember -- please, look this way or at the Judges. You said you spoke with him after the war. Do you recall speaking with him during the war in respect to the flow of refugees through his border post?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I spoke to him as this flood of refugees occurred. It was after the war that I spoke to him, after the arrival at and departure from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that on the 27th of March when the first big group of refugees arrived at his border post at Vranica [sic] he called his headquarters in Belgrade to ask what he was to do about them. Were you aware of that call?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact this was going on at Vrbnica border crossing, and I know that a decision had been taken to allow those people to cross into a neighbouring territory, but I don't remember the commander calling me personally. Possibly it was one of the other officials from his department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. He also said that he sent a report about it, and that report you have here, it's P3086. Now, this is a report that he sent about the first big group of refugees that he saw in his experience and he sent it up to the headquarters. Could you have a look at it, please, and tell me if you recall seeing that at the time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to see this document at the time because my administration was at various locations in Belgrade, and each administration dealt independently with problems such as these and took their own decisions whenever it was impossible to get in touch with me because this was at a time of air-raid alerts and for the most part we were not in our offices. I can't remember seeing this document specifically, but I'm aware of this particular development.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this document -- this official note signed by Lieutenant Ognjenovic says that this group of Albanians, mostly women and elderly, reported that their ID cards had been taken from them and kept at the Prizren SUP. Did anyone make you in your leadership capacity aware of what the chief of this border station was reporting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know about this particular development is that there was a large group of persons women, children, and elderly who were trying to leave the territory because of the danger they were facing back in their respective places of residence on account of the ongoing war. That was the reason they stated the decision was taken to allow them to leave as long as the neighbouring country of course agreed to take them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you are not answering my question directly. Did it come to your knowledge or were you told that the chief of the police station reported that his information was that the IDs and documents of these 94 elderly and women, elderly persons and women, were taken away by the SUP police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing to the effect that their ID documents had been seized by members of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The person at the headquarters in Belgrade who received this document, what would have been their duty, what ought they to have done in respect to a report that a SUP was taking away ID cards from that number of civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any person receiving, a person receiving a report like this after the fact, additionally because their report could not have been dispatched at the time of this event, and this person would have been under an obligation to pass this along to the relevant office within the administration, somebody would have verified this information and would have established the reason why the ID card which could not have been taken from any person, unless obviously this was a case of forgery or something like that. No document can just be taken away like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to your answer. Look at the top of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you find a suitable time to interrupt, please. If you feel you have to finish this, finish it; but if you can interrupt it, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at the top of the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could scroll to the top of the B/C/S and to the top of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see something indicating that there is a print as to the time and date it was sent by fax from phone number 7445 March 27, 1999, at 3.48 p.m. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the fax number is 7145. That machine was used to send this document, but I can't see the number of the recipient. I see the date and the time, though, 27th of March, 3.48.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. As far as administration is concerned, and it's only for that reason, have you any estimate of how long you will be with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Half-hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So not even the full session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will attempt to leave enough time for re-examination if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn now, Mr. Dujkovic, until 2.30. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can now continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we left off, Mr. Dujkovic, we were looking at a document sent to you by Mr. Ognjenovic, and I think you agreed that it was sent just about contemporaneously with the events that it described. So is it then your evidence that notwithstanding that, nothing was done from your department in respect to the allegation that the SUP of Prizren had taken away these people's ID cards?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding this, you say that this document was sent to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it wasn't. I'd never even seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm saying it was sent -- I'm saying the evidence is from Mr. Ognjenovic, that it was sent to the headquarters in Belgrade, that is to your headquarters in Belgrade. All I'm saying is that you said that the document was dealing with events that had occurred long before, and I showed you that the document was sent just about the same time as the events. All I'm asking is: Having regarding to that, now that you see it was sent to Belgrade just about the same time as the events, can you not recall whether or not your department did anything about those allegations in the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that we did anything about that in the sense of verifying these allegations that ID cards had been seized. Based on this document I cannot tell that it was ever sent to Belgrade because the number here is entirely different, the number is 7145 and there is no such number existing in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness Ognjenovic said that it was sent to his headquarters in Belgrade, that is to your office in Belgrade. Is there any reason not to believe him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly believe what he says and I believe that that's what he did; however, our administration was not based in one place but rather at various locations across Belgrade and I can't remember specifically where that section of the administration that was in charge of that located at the time or indeed whether they received this and how. The ministry building itself had been evacuated because of bomb threats or air-strike threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I may move on, you knew at the time Branislav Mitrovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of one of our stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was a commander of a station or was he during the NATO intervention the chief of the department of border affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the air-strikes he was commander of a border police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He later became chief of the department for border affairs, did he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the air-strikes and when Mr. Lukic took over the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember which police station he was chief of during the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's close to the border with Romania?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it actually straddles the border with Romania, but it's on the right-hand bank of the River Danube. It covered a border crossing there and another road crossing the border near the hydro-electric plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, he gave a statement in 2001 in which he said that on or about the 6th of April, 1999, he was summoned by the Kladovo OUP chief to a location where a truck with corpses of many people, Albanians, was being pulled out of the Danube. And he and other members of the MUP had to get involved in organizing the retrieval of the truck and the movement of the bodies. And in that statement he said that he telephoned you about it, and you told him to give the police who were moving the bodies whatever assistance he could. Do you recall that phone call from Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what happened, and I know that he informed me about it, he informed me about the fact that a lorry had been found on the banks of the Danube near Kladovo and I can't remember the exact whereabouts. He said some dead bodies had been found, and I realized immediately that this was a lorry that had swerved off the road and ended up by the roadside, since this is a road that runs roughly parallel to the riverbank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did he tell you how many dead bodies were in that truck?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no reference to dead bodies. He just said that the site was secured and that local SUP people were now there. He said some people had been killed and he said this was some sort of a refrigerated lorry carrying goods, that was my understanding at the time, some sort of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we should have that answer revised by CLSS, that's the answer at line 16 at page 3 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You now say that he did not tell you about dead bodies being found in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me. I only found out about the dead bodies from the press in 2001, that was the first time. He told me about what had happened and that his assistance was required -- not specifically, but if necessary. And I did what we usually do when one of our neighbouring bodies needs assistance, especially since this was a border police station which as part of its standard-issue equipment also had a rather large vessel, a boat in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why would police station chief Mitrovic tell you that this lorry contained goods when, in fact, it contained dead bodies? Because you're now saying that he would have lied to you about the contents of the lorry. Why would he have lied to you about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to him at the time, and at no time before 2001 had I been aware of the fact that there had been dead bodies inside that lorry, he didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the question is because he --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And perhaps I should indicate to the Court that the document is P584, but I'm not sure if it came in under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said quite specifically in this document that he contributed some of his people, that is, some of your people in this process of retrieving the bodies, and he did so after you told him to cooperate and to help. On what basis would he not tell you that there were bodies or -- well, maybe we should define what we mean by goods. You said that he told you that there were goods in the lorry. What sort of goods did he tell you was in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember the conversation correctly, he said there was a lorry involved that had driven off the road, flown off the road. There were people who had been killed, purportedly in a serious traffic accident or something like that, it's normally down to the local SUP to secure the scene of accident, to provide assistance, and when I said "assistance," I believed what what was implied at the time was technical assistance because this involved water, it involved a river, that's why. Otherwise, I have no idea whether there was any assistance at a later stage that was provided because I never learned any more about this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were not apprised by him as to what the goods were that were in the lorry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not share any detail of this with me. He never mentioned dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now getting back to what I asked you, do you know of any reason why one of your police station chiefs would concoct this story and tell you in that phone call?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any reason, but not all type of information is shared over the phone, especially not at the time. There were probably mobile phones involved, we were not where we were supposed to be, not at our original seat, because our building had been destroyed in the air-strikes. This sort of information is actually not conveyed in any great detail. A brief account is more common, otherwise he would have had every responsibility to assist his colleagues in any way and that was a well-known thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean in his statement he says that the refrigerator lorry was full of flesh, there were corpses, and he returned to the police -- to the site where the lorry was, and the border police - that is, your staff - remained at the scene. Now, is that a detail that you'd expect him to fail to tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what he did there at the time, specifically I know he briefly informed me about what had happened, that an event had taken place, that appropriate authorities were there on the ground, and that he was in a position to assist if necessary. At the time he -- or they probably didn't even know specifically what had occurred or what this was about. I knew there was a vehicle, I knew there was a body of water nearby, and I knew that there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the B/C/S original the witness is using the word "mrtvi," which means dead people or dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And that assistance was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you never heard about it until it became splashed in the press in 2001, I think that's your evidence. Did any of the investigators in the working group that sought to investigate these bodies in 2001 interview you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any working group and no one interviewed me about this. First I hear of it in terms of me knowing anything about any bodies being in that lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we can go on. Yesterday - and this is at page 23346 of the transcript - you said, and you said you were making assumptions and it was a speculation, but you said that in respect to the people who left or who left Kosovo, the Kosovar Albanians who left Kosovo in -- during the NATO intervention in 1999, there would have had to be an agreement put in place between Serbia or the FRY and the countries to which they went to facilitate their return. While you were in the ministry, do you know any such attempts to agree or work out a framework for their return prior to the arrival of UNMIK in Kosovo in latter part of 1999?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That possibility was not something that was being considered at the time, since no conditions were in place for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to Sadija Sadiku, you were shown a document 6D1324 which said that there was no record of her in Serbia, of her existence in Serbia. Let me ask you a hypothetical question. If it was established that she was, in fact, issued with a birth certificate by the Serbian authorities or the authorities of the FRY, how is it possible that now they could issue a document indicating that in all of these records her name is not found?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object at this point. Do we have this birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was said to be a hypothetical question, Mr. Lukic. It's not directly related to the individual yet, so on that basis it seems appropriate to ask the question, see where it's going, and you can object again if it raises a matter that you think ought to be objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document says that no such person is to be found in the MUP files, the birth registers are not part of the MUP files, that's a birth register office and that's a different ministry. You asked me about a birth certificate being issued and can this person obtain the document and go back to their place of birth. No, it's all about citizenship. This person must be a national. The fact of birth does not imply citizenship. A person can, for example, have his or her citizenship revoked somewhere in the meantime and maybe citizenship was never awarded to begin with at birth since citizenship can be awarded on a number of different bases. So this fact of citizenship is the only criterion in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you are going a little bit beyond what I was asking about. Your answer suggests that the records of the birth registry would not be used or would not be transferred to the records of the MUP, that is what it suggests. But I thought you said yesterday that when someone is born they have to be registered, and that office registers it and the document has to be sent to the MUP in Belgrade in order for, among other things, a national ID number. I'm not sure if I have the expression correct, but the 13-digit number to be issued. I think that's what you said yesterday. So I will ask you the question again. Having regarding to what you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- if this person, or if there is a birth certificate for this person, how can you explain that document which says that she does not come up in any of the records of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this question concrete enough to see that birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours but he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're still in the hypothetical situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- but he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the question's not a hypothetical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If there is a birth certificate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but how can you explain that document which says she doesn't come up, so you're saying: How do you explain this document if she doesn't have a birth certificate. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If she does have a birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If she does, yes. Well, you would need to have some basis for saying she had one before there would be any point in that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the good-faith basis I have for asking this question is this: We have contact with the witness and we are trying to procure her birth certificate. But I don't think we would want to procure the birth certificate and then -- I don't know if we would want to call for this witness to return to ask him about it. So I would submit that the appropriate way to put it to the witness and to give the witness an opportunity to comment on it is to ask the hypothetical, because I don't have the birth certificate in my hands. But I expect to have it after the witness is passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that the witness says she has a birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness said that she had one so we are trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That she had one. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I still think that without having that birth certificate this witness cannot comment in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are satisfied that the explanation given justifies asking the question, but we do note that if nothing is produced to substantiate the existence at one time of a birth certificate then it is difficult to see how this could weigh in any manner in our decision. However, in light of the possibility that the situation could change we will allow the question to be asked. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If this person did, in fact, at one time have a birth certificate issued by the appropriate organs of the FRY, how would you explain that response, saying that she is not recorded anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of different possibilities. For example, the following situation, the relevant body failed to submit to the SUP information on this person's birth since she does not have a birth register number -- insufficient information was provided in order to ascertain that this person was actually recorded. Should be required for this is the citizen's personal identification number and then this person's data would have been recorded, but I think the same files were looked at and nothing was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case, this person and persons in her position would have -- would face serious impediments in trying to return to Kosovo, would she not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that such cases were rare. This is probably an administrative error or perhaps a different kind of problem, maybe incomplete information. Any person who was in the files in as far as they were Yugoslav citizens were allowed to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the person involved has been a witness in this case, and therefore there must have been some other -- there must have been a reason for you leading this evidence other than some technical point about registration or is it wrong to think that there must be some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That we wanted to impeach this witness because she claimed that her documents were taken away from her and we wanted to prove that she had never had any documents. Maybe she was not from Kosovo at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have here -- and I'm moving on to the German decisions or the decisions from the German courts that you commented about. And I have here a document which I took down off the internet and I would like to read a couple sentences from it and ask you if that is your experience. This is a Human Rights Watch World report --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would just object but not strongly because we received this document only today. But since Mr. Bakrac presented his documents, we just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he's remaining silent, so ... Mr. Stamp, has this been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's no number for it yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this report the Human Rights Watch organization says: "Most western European states heeded the United Nations High Commission for Refugees' plea to halt expulsions of rejected Kosovo Albanian asylum seekers; however, Germany and Switzerland refused to ban expulsions for the first five months of the conflict. Together they expelled hundreds to Kosovo." Firstly, you indicated that your understanding was like 150.000 people were sent to Kosovo. Is it not a matter of hundreds? Does this refresh your recollection that over this period of time there were hundreds?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that in the 1990s in western European countries, according the estimates of those countries there were, roughly speaking, a total of 150.000 people from Serbia, most of them from Kosovo, who were staying in those countries illegally, although from our point of view the departure of these persons may have been perfectly legal. These for the most part were false asylum seekers and illegal immigrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It -- the report goes on to say in respect to these people who were sent back to Kosovo: "Where upon return many were detained and interrogated and some were severely beaten, according to interviews with Human Rights Watch." Wasn't that the fate of many --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would, Your Honour, object at this point because we established during these proceedings that data allegedly collected by Human Rights Watch --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just let Mr. Lukic finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we objected when Mr. Abrahams was here and testified that actually they didn't interview people, they claimed that they interviewed them, and we object to any kind of conclusions drawn from the allegedly taken by the Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- he's the person responsible for the police involved in receiving these people. There is an allegation here that contrary to what some court may have found in order to expel the people back to Kosovo, when they returned they were detained, interrogated, and some severely beaten. Now, he should be entitled to comment on it. That's all I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. The objection taken by Mr. Lukic is misconceived. There is a clear difference between the Trial Chamber admitting documents in the course of the Prosecution case as evidence in support of that case and the situation of documents used in cross-examination which we've repeatedly explained can only be admitted to the extent -- at this stage in the Prosecution case can only -- sorry, at this stage in the trial can only be admitted in support of the Prosecution case to the extent that they are actually accepted by a witness. So there's no question here at this moment and at this stage in the course of this cross-examination of this being admitted independently and free-standing to contradict anything that the witness might say. Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well -- thank you, Your Honours. I wonder having regard to the objection being voiced in the presence of the witness if there's any point in asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there is point in this instance, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that an accurate reflection of what occurred to many of these people who were sent back to Kosovo, that they were detained, interrogated, and many severely beaten?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the return of these persons to Serbia, negotiations were held for several years with the appropriate authorities of the said states. Particular attention was paid to the fact that solid guarantees should be provided that nothing would happen to these persons. If a person had committed a crime and was therefore on the run, then perhaps it could have been -- this person could have been handed over to the appropriate authorities; but everything we were doing was supervised by the representatives of these states. They could be at the airports of Belgrade and Pristina themselves, and we organized transport for these persons to their places of residence. To be more specific, if we could not get to their actual place of residence, these persons would get 50 German marks in order to get a ride to their homes. The commission that was mentioned yesterday or today, I'm sorry, at any rate reacted to any case, even an individual case, of mistreatment of persons, even if it was just because they returned from Germany. Since I was in charge of this particular work, I state with full responsibility that persons were not mistreated because they were returned from Germany. Whether somebody had some problems after that, that I cannot speak of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Through your discussions with the members of the expert committee, did you learn of money being given by the German government to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees to assist in the returning of Kosovo Albanian refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know about any money that the German government gave to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, but I know that governments financed this project and that our government got a donation in order to have this project carried through. We got computers and other equipment so that we could process applications more quickly. I apologise. Also all the transport costs from the German airports to our airport and police escorts included, all of that was paid for by the German government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of other governments refusing to return Albanian asylum seekers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that. I know that negotiations were carried out with more than ten states and that these negotiations had reached different stages. It was not our request that these persons should be returned, it was the request of the governments of those countries. They wanted to rid themselves of these persons who did not have a basis for receiving protection because their basic human rights and freedoms had not been jeopardized at their homes and their lives were not under threat at their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying you're not aware of any country halting the expulsion of Kosovo Albanian asylum seekers? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. What I hear in the interpretation is the word "expulsion." This is an organized return of persons to their homes through a coordinated action by the appropriate organs of two countries. I am not aware of any country doing something like that -- well, quite simply a country that was not interested in doing this did not negotiate with us and did not address us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, may I put it this way: Were you aware that there were other countries in Europe who refused to send back Kosovar Albanians because they were dissatisfied with the human rights situation in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that because as far as I know our government did not send requests to have these persons returned. It was these other states that took the initiative. We cannot know of any such thing unless there is an initiative launched by the other country.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll give that document an IC number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I should have indicated that it was uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, it is. Well, the only part that's of any relevance to the case to put the questions in context is the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, it was uploaded as P3114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp, I -- if you know the names of some of those countries you can suggest those to the witness who refused to send the persons you mentioned, in case you know the names of those countries. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe I do, but I could suggest one that is not correct. But what I will suggest is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That apart from Switzerland and Germany, is it not true that all or most of, if not all, of the countries in the EU refused to send back Kosovar Albanians to Serbia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that bilateral agreements were concluded with a great many countries on the return of these persons, and while I worked at the administration an agreement was actually carried through with only two countries, Germany and Switzerland. Today I know that an agreement had been signed with the European Union. So probably all the bilateral agreements were included in this agreement with the European Union, that is to say all member states of the EU. There is an agreement on re-admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this bilateral agreement with the EU signed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe this year or last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But, Mr. Dujkovic, we're talking about the period up to March 1999, which is what counsel asked you about, and what I'm putting to you is that apart from Switzerland and Germany, most, if not all, of the countries of the EU refused to send Kosovar Albanians back to Serbia. Isn't that your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of some country deciding not to return these persons. I just know that we carried this agreement through with two countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, yesterday you were telling us where the border crossings or border police stations were that might be relevant, and you were translated in English as saying that: "There was an extra border police station near Pristina." Now, were you referring there simply to the airport or were you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was referring to the airport as a border crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was it that provided the border police service between Montenegro and Albania and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, with Montenegro at that time we did not have a border service because there were no border crossings. As for the border crossings towards Albania, policemen from the border police stations worked there, those that belonged to the Ministry of the Interior, or to be more precise to the administration of the border police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand my question. I'm interested in people crossing from Montenegro into either Albania or Bosnia, which organization provided the border police service for these crossings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you're asking me about Montenegro, who provided this in Montenegro? I don't know about Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have some general knowledge about this that in Montenegro, like in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know the regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. It just seemed to me that -- slightly odd, but perhaps not, that the border is controlled by the republican Ministry of the Interior and not the Federal Ministry of the Interior. And I wondered if it was the same situation in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the past 40 years, every republic was responsible for checking border crossings and for providing in-depth security of the state border. And on the line of the border itself security for the border was provided by the border service of the Army of Yugoslavia that was a federal institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can understand an outsider's confusion when part of the system for doing a similar and closely related job is federal and another part is republican. And I just want to know if that was universal and that seems to be what you're saying. What I'd like to know, though, is whether you know for sure that in the year -- the years between 1993 -- I suppose 1992 and 1999 that the system in Montenegro was the same as the system in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that the border units of the Army of Yugoslavia were securing the state border towards Albania, in Montenegro too, but not towards Kosovo and towards Serbia, only towards Albania. Later probably it was Croatia too, or rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. I don't know exactly whether over there they have the republican institution checking border crossings. In some republics it's even done at a lower level, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the fairly senior position you held, I assume that you were expected to understand where the MUP staff for Kosovo fitted into the administration of the Republic of Serbia. Is that a fair assumption?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where did it fit in and what was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew of Radovan Vucurevic on the staff as a representative of this line of work. I as a leading person in the administration that I headed at the time, I did not have any other direct contacts with the staff members or with the head of the staff. I resolved all problems directly, perhaps with the involvement of Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So as far as you were concerned then, could you simply ignore its existence, it had absolutely no relevance to your life and work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that our representative on the staff, Mr. Vucurevic, was useful in that position because he enabled us to have him take direct part in resolving some more complex subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he needed to be told that more because he had no idea why he was there. You've talked in very eloquent language about the job, but what was he actually doing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no need to involve Mr. Vucurevic very often because we resolved all problems directly with the leaders of the regional SUPs or with our station commanders. Mr. Vucurevic only got this one specific task, to be an "officer" or even without quotation marks, liaison officer with the representatives of international humanitarian organizations. Our representative from the administration had direct contact with the representatives of the international organizations. This was Radovan Vucurevic, who was a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, re-exam -- Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for taking up time this afternoon, but there is something that remains unclear from Mr. Stamp's questions and Judge Chowhan asked about this too. Is Mr. Stamp perhaps referring to the Albanians that we were looking for through Interpol and then they would not hand them over to us as crime suspects? But that the Serbs was looking for Serbs or Albanians who went to work abroad without papers, that did not happen, so perhaps that's the problem. At this moment we are talking about the re-admission of 180.000 Roma, Kurds, and I don't know who else who are supposed to return to our country because it is from our territory that they entered the European Union. Take my word for it, 180.000 persons. The ministry is dealing with this. If this matters to the Trial Chamber, if they want to establish that, I really have to tell you that as a state we did not even ask them to return Serbs to the country, let alone others, Albanians, et cetera. As for the police, yes, crime suspects and people like that, yes. If this really matters for this particular case, then it really should be cleared up. That would be all and I thank you for the time and I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No need to apologise unless you waste our time. The -- there are two points arising from that, one is that the witness I think has already dealt with the question of why the knowledge he has relates to Germany and Switzerland with whom these negotiations took place. And secondly, you realize that the issue has only concerned us because it was raised by Mr. Bakrac and we are doing our best to make sure that both sides have an adequate opportunity to present what little material they appear to have on the issue. Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Hopefully we'll finish until the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, I'll have a few more questions for you. First I would like to ask you to look at document 6D475.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about this document in paragraph 20 of your written statement, and today my colleague Mr. Stamp asked you about this. And on the last page of this document it says Obrad Stevanovic. You said that it was signed by Obrad Stevanovic. I'm going to ask you the following now, or rather, what was said then was that this was your speculation, speculation on your part. Did this document have to be signed in order to be sent or could it have been sent like this, unsigned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be signed in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next document that I'm interested in is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would suggest there's something wrong with the English translation because the wording of that suggests that someone else could sign it for him. The word "for" is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, the English translation is actually wrong. It just say: "Assistant minister Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic." There is no "for" in Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, now, it may not actually matter to the point Mr. Stamp was making, because his point I think related to whether it was within Stevanovic's authority to be giving -- to be dealing with this. And at the time it didn't seem to me to matter whether it said "for" or not, but we will note what you say about the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I see where the confusion probably lies in the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, could you please open 6D464. Have you found it? Mr. Stamp asked you whether the MUP staff had received reports about crimes and other issues relevant for the security, other incidents, whether they received those reports from the SUPs. But is this document about reporting or about asking permission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is actually all about seeking approval for instituting proceedings against the police officer, because proceedings could not be instituted against the police officer before a report to that effect was sent to his line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this different from ordinary reporting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is seeking approval, so this is different indeed from merely reporting about events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this approval for filing a criminal report, could it have been sought from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the staff did not have any jurisdiction over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the approval for the filing of a criminal report, could it have been sought from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on e-court Exhibit 6D770.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First let me ask you, did you know how the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija actually operated in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was partly aware of it to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the chief of the public security sector, could he have ordered the MUP staff members to do some tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document, in the first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to the Law on Domicile and Place of Residence of Citizens, the rules on forms and manner of keeping records on domicile and place of residence of citizens, decree on domicile and place of residence of citizens during a state of war, and the dispatch of the public security department or sector, the following action must be taken." Any further action by the MUP staff in this case, would it be based on the dispatch from the public security sector and the legislation listed above --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that just is a leading question that -- the answer to now which now wouldn't help us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Micropohone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on what basis did the MUP staff actually act in this case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in this case the MUP staff invoked the dispatch from the chief of the sector, and I think that this dispatch had already been sent to all the organs in the territory of Serbia including Kosovo at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that dispatch, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know that off the top of my head, but I can perhaps make some assumptions. If I could perhaps be shown this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we don't, we don't have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, a dispatch -- I mean, a dispatch presumably could contain a number of different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the tasks that are listed in this memo from the staff, the staff would not receive orders to do that. The MUP would issue orders to the SUPs directly, to its subordinate organs directly, and the MUP staff would merely be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's you putting the cart before the horse, if I may say. Would the MUP issue orders to the SUPs in a dispatch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be issued -- those orders would be issued in the dispatch, but the MUP would -- MUP staff would receive information. Since this is in my line of work, it would never happen that an order would be issued to the MUP staff to take certain measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but what I want to be clear about is this: If you were referring to an instruction sent by the MUP to SUP chiefs directly, would you describe that as a dispatch when you were writing something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a dispatch is one form of communication, using the communication equipment that is fairly quick, the teleprinter, this is what we call a dispatch. You can also send it using couriers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's been some evidence which I can't remember the detail of at this point about the appropriate language to describe an instruction or direction given by the Ministry of the Interior to a chief of a SUP. What was the word that was appropriate for such a direction or instruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Nalog."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is "nalog"? And the word "zapovest" is not used?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Zapovest," could be but it's different. "Zapovest" -- actually "naradjenje" -- not, "zapovest" in police we have "naradjenje" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "Naradjenje," yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- order and "nalog" order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that it would be appropriate where directions - and you've heard the language we've been discussing just now, when directions were being given by the MUP to chiefs of SUPs, it would be appropriate when referring to that to talk about a dispatch; that's your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this kind of order, "nalog," can be sent in a dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, it would obviously assist our understanding of all of this if that dispatch can be produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fila just pushed me to work hard and find that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well that's the real answer to -- not necessarily the real answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but it would advance our knowledge of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have it in our documents, but we'll try to find it somewhere in MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course you have no obligation to find it. All I'm suggesting to you is that it may assist us, and that of course applies to the Prosecution as well if they can lay their hands on it, then it would assist us. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we find this document, or rather, until we find this document I will try to now use abuse your knowledge. What is a dispatch, is this kind of document or is this just a manner in which documents are communicated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the kind of document that is sent using teleprinters or in a telegram, this kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before that is a written document drafted and it is then typed into the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whoever is sending a dispatch, first drafts the document, signs the document, and then this is sent to the communications service, which sends it on. The signed copy is kept in the file in order to prove that the -- whoever drafted and sent the initial document complied with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Dujkovic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal here to give evidence. You can now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- before we move on, just indicate to the Court, it's probably not the right time, but for what it's worth, counsel did say that the witness Sadiku said that her identification card or her identification documents were taken away. That is not precisely correct. The witness said speaking of a group of people that she was with that their identification card, referring to the group, identification cards, passports, whatever we had on us, that's what she said, were taken away. Just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. That's always a matter for interpretation in due course. Mr. Lukic, you have one more witness allocated for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the indications are you won't finish that witness in one day unless you've revised your prognosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Ivetic is working with the judge and I really don't know what his time schedule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I was going to say is if ten minutes today will help you, then we'll start; if it would make no difference, then we'll finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't make any difference, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you're right. Does that mean, though, that you really don't know the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also cannot calculate if other Defence teams have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but your estimate's three hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in a four-hour day which suggests it's unlikely, no matter what the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Highly unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're happy to adjourn now if that is convenient to you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which means that we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this court.
